title: Louisville and Portland Canal
summary: Opened in 1830, the Louisville and Portland Canal let boats bypass the Falls of the Ohio, the only barrier to navigation from Pittsburgh to New Orleans.
bodyMarkdown:
The [Falls of the Ohio](/stories/falls-of-the-ohio/) are a stretch of rapids and rock ledges at Louisville. They were the only real barrier to boats on the whole Ohio River, from Pittsburgh all the way down to New Orleans. Except for a few weeks of high water in spring, cargo had to be unloaded above the falls, hauled around them by wagon, and loaded onto another boat below.

That portage helped build Louisville and its neighbors, Portland and Shippingport. Local draymen and warehouse owners made money on every load. Merchants upriver in Pittsburgh and Cincinnati saw it differently. The delay raised their costs, and shipments piled up whenever the water rose.

People talked about a canal for decades. As early as 1781 the town trustees of Louisville asked Virginia for the right to dig one. Kentucky and Indiana both chartered canal companies in 1805, but nothing came of either. In 1825 Kentucky chartered the private Louisville and Portland Canal Company, and the federal government bought a large share of its stock.

Work began on March 1, 1826. Crews cut the channel through solid rock along the Kentucky bank. The canal opened in 1830. As built, it was 1.9 miles long and 64 feet wide, and it ended in a three-flight lock that lifted boats a total of 26 feet. It was the [first major improvement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisville_and_Portland_Canal) completed on a major river in the United States.

The canal was an instant success, but steamboats kept getting bigger, and the locks were soon too small. Tolls ran high, and over the rest of the century the federal government bought out the private owners and took over the work. The canal was widened and the locks rebuilt more than once.

## Kentucky today

In 1962 the modernized canal and locks were renamed the [McAlpine Locks and Dam](https://grokipedia.com/page/McAlpine_Locks_and_Dam). Barge tows still use the canal, which runs along the Kentucky bank beside Shippingport Island. The map pin marks the lock site at the downstream end.
Source: [Louisville and Portland Canal Locks and Dam (ASCE landmark)](https://www.asce.org/about-civil-engineering/history-and-heritage/historic-landmarks/louisville-and-portland-canal-locks-and-dam)
